metadata.title: The Wrong Abstraction
metadata.abstract_summary: The specific, credible failure mode this gap-analysis pass was asked to find: unifying code across call sites that turn out to have different needs degrades predictably — parameters and conditionals accumulate until the "shared" version is neither coherent nor maintainable — and Metz's named remedy is to deliberately re-duplicate it first, then re-abstract from what the duplication reveals.

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text: Metz's central line, quoted directly: "duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction." The essay traces a specific, repeatable sequence: duplicated code gets extracted into a shared abstraction; a new requirement arrives that doesn't quite fit; a programmer adds a parameter or a conditional branch to accommodate it rather than rethinking the abstraction; this repeats with each subsequent requirement until the shared code is a condition-laden object that serves no call site cleanly. She attributes the failure to persist past the point it should have been reversed to sunk-cost reasoning — complex code looks like it represents real effort, which creates pressure to preserve rather than unwind it.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: A practice essay grounded in a single worked example from the author's own consulting/teaching experience (a Ruby codebase), not an empirical study across multiple codebases or teams. The argument is demonstrated through one detailed before/after case rather than measured across a sample.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text: Single source, read directly in full for this note. The essay is explicitly anecdotal in method — one illustrative case, not a study — and does not claim statistical generality; its authority rests on the specificity and plausibility of the mechanism it describes (parameter creep, sunk-cost pressure) rather than on measured prevalence. It also does not address the organisational-scale version of this same risk — shared code deliberately maintained *across separate repositories*, which is this vault's own motivating case — only the single-codebase version of premature shared abstraction. The extrapolation from "one file, many call sites" to "one shared tool, several independent repositories" is this note's own inference, not a claim the essay itself makes.
